I. 
INTRODUCTION 
 
In this order, the Vermont Public Utility Commission (“Commission”) partially approves 
Green Mountain Power Corporation’s (“GMP”) proposed 7.06% rate increase and a new Multi-
Year Regulation Plan (“MYRP”), both to take effect on October 1, 2026.   
 
This order reflects a balance between two vital but at times competing interests.  We are 
acutely aware of the financial challenges confronting GMP’s ratepayers in today’s economy.  We 
are mindful that a rate increase—at any level—imposes a substantial burden on many of those 
customers, particularly those with limited incomes.  The inflationary costs that are hitting all 
Vermonters—higher health care, fuel, and other expenses—are also affecting companies, 
including GMP.  Electric utilities are allowed to recover reasonable costs to provide service to 
their customers, and GMP’s increased costs are reflected in the rate increase approved today.  
The rate increase and MYRP approved today also seek to balance affordability with ensuring a 
regulatory structure that allows GMP to access the financial resources necessary to operate in a 
capital-intensive industry.  
At the same time, GMP is confronting novel operational challenges caused by more 
frequent and severe storm events.  It is becoming increasingly apparent that changing climate 
patterns necessitate new investments and hardening of the grid to ensure that GMP continues to 
provide safe and reliable service to its customers.

In deciding these cases, we seek to set a balanced approach to mitigate immediate 
ratepayer impacts while enabling GMP to continue investing in new resilience upgrades.  
Throughout this order we discuss in detail various components of GMP’s proposed MYRP and 
overall cost of service.  We dedicate a significant portion of our discussion sections to the 
interplay between affordability, GMP’s proposed resilience projects, and GMP’s financial risk 
while operating under the MYRP.   
 
Our resolution of the various underlying issues in these cases will require GMP to file a 
revised cost of service that reflects a 9.04% authorized rate of return on equity and authorizes 
GMP to spend $113.2 million on new resilience projects over the four-year term of the MYRP.  
GMP will need to recalculate the actual rate increase based on the decisions we make in this 
order, but we anticipate that GMP’s proposed rate increase will be reduced from 7.06% to 
approximately 5.5%.

III. 
PUBLIC COMMENTS 
 
Over the course of these proceedings, the Commission received 52 written comments 
from members of the public.  We also received comments from the public during the public 
hearing held on December 11, 2026. 
 
With one exception, all of the comments raised opposition to and concerns about GMP’s 
proposed rate increase.  Many of the comments expressed frustration about GMP’s current rates 
and raised concerns about the affordability of a rate increase.  There were several discrete issues 
addressed by the comments, including the efficiency charge, electrification, net-metering, and 
executive compensation. 
 
In setting GMP’s rates, we take a comprehensive look at the company’s underlying 
expenses to determine an appropriate amount of revenue that GMP must have the opportunity to 
generate to operate its network safely and reliability.  This is not an easy task.  It entails the 
review of hundreds of pages of testimony, numerous exhibits, and detailed financial documents.  
Our review must also be completed within the framework of existing state and federal law, 
which imposes various requirements and limitations on the breadth and scope of our review.  
These requirements are discussed in detail throughout this order.   
 
We strongly encourage members of the public to review this order in its entirety to gain a 
detailed understanding of the rate setting process and our resolution of these cases, which are 
exhaustive in scope.  We also stress that the public comments that we received, particularly the 
concerns expressed about affordability, have had considerable influence on the outcome of these 
cases and on many of the decisions we made regarding GMP’s rates.   
IV. 
THE PROPOSED MULTI-YEAR REGULATION PLAN 
Legal Standard 
 
Title 30, Section 218d authorizes the Commission to approve alternative regulation plans 
for electric and natural gas companies.  The Commission, on its own motion or on the motion of 
the Department or a company operating under an alternative regulation plan, may investigate any 
alternative regulation plan that is in effect and, following notice and an opportunity for hearing, 
may terminate or modify the alternative regulation plan upon a finding of good cause.1 
 
1 30 V.S.A. § 218d(i).

To approve a petition to approve a new alternative regulation plan or amend an existing 
plan, the Commission must find that the proposed form of alternative regulation will: 
(1) establish a system of regulation in which . . . companies have clear incentives 
to provide least-cost energy service to their customers;  
(2) provide just and reasonable rates for service to all classes of customers; 
(3) deliver safe and reliable service; 
(4) offer incentives for innovations and improved performance that advance state 
energy policy such as increasing reliance on Vermont-based renewable energy 
and decreasing the extent to which the financial success of distribution utilities 
between rate cases is linked to increased sales to end use customers and may be 
threatened by decreases in those sales; 
(5) promote improved quality of service, reliability, and service choices; 
(6) encourage innovation in the provision of service; 
(7) establish a reasonably balanced system of risks and rewards that encourages the 
company to operate as efficiently as possible using sound management 
practices; and 
(8) provide a reasonable opportunity, under sound and economical management, to 
earn a fair rate of return, provided such opportunity must be consistent with 
flexible design of alternative regulation and with the inclusion of effective 
financial incentives in such alternatives.2 
In the case of an investor-owned company such as GMP, the Commission will approve 
an alternative regulation plan only if we find that the plan “will not have an adverse impact on 
the electric company’s eligibility for rate-regulated accounting in accordance with generally 
accepted accounting standards if applicable; and reasonably preserve the availability of equity 
and debt capital resources to the company on favorable terms and conditions.”3 
Finally, alternative regulation may include changes or alternatives to traditional ratemaking 
procedures, standards, and mechanisms if the Commission finds that alternative regulation will 
promote the public good and will support the required findings in 30 V.S.A. § 218d(a).4

Discussion 
 
At the outset of our discussion of the proposed MYRP, we emphasize that our review is 
based on a wholistic approach to the plan.  Throughout this order, we analyze discrete 
components of the proposed MYRP in separate discussion sections.  However, our review of 
these individual components is informed by the broader context of GMP’s comprehensive 
proposal.  We consider how each component fits within the overall structure of the plan.  In 
doing so, we are mindful that a change in one aspect of GMP’s proposal may have a corollary 
impact on other components of the plan.  This is particularly true for the elements of the plan that 
have a stronger impact on GMP’s overall financial risk, particularly in setting the Earnings 
Sharing Adjustment Mechanism (“ESAM”) and the underlying return on equity (“ROE”).   
 
Ultimately, our objective in reviewing GMP’s proposed MYRP is to ensure that the plan 
satisfies the Section 218d criteria listed above.  This analysis requires careful consideration of 
the various benefits and potential drawbacks for both GMP and its ratepayers.  Our discussion 
sections below highlight several areas where there is a tension between those interests.  Our 
resolution of these issues remains firmly fixed to the Section 218d criteria.  However, it is 
important to emphasize that our focus is also framed by the statutory standard that GMP’s rates

Discussion 
Return on Equity 
 
We first address the parties’ arguments on the authorized ROE components of the 
MYRP.  The Department recommends that the Commission transition away from annual, 
formulaic adjustments to GMP’s ROE.  Instead, the Department argues that the Commission 
should establish an ROE that remains fixed for the full term of the plan.  The Department asserts 
that a fixed ROE will reduce both ratepayer and shareholder risk and “ensure that the balance 
struck by the Commission” in adopting an ROE in the rate case “remains intact over the course 
of the Plan.”9 
 
We decline to adopt the Department’s recommendation to fix the ROE for the full term of 
the MYRP.  Establishing a fixed ROE would lead to a greater degree of rate stability and

certainty for GMP’s ratepayers.  However, we note that the broader economy is currently 
experiencing high inflation, there is volatility in both the equity and debt markets, and recent 
global events have resulted in further uncertainty and disruptions to energy markets.  Locking the 
ROE at the rate we set today could result in an ROE that falls out of sync with actual market 
performance and expectations and could, in turn, cause customers to overpay or affect GMP’s 
ability to access capital at reasonable terms.  Considering these economic conditions, which 
carry a substantially higher degree of uncertainty than when we approved the current ROE 
formula, we conclude that a fixed ROE would expose both ratepayers and GMP to an 
unnecessary degree of financial risk.   
 
The parties in this case also presented testimony and arguments raising concerns about 
continued reliance on U.S. Treasury yields as a benchmark for ROE adjustments.  This approach 
has served as a reasonable proxy for assessing perceived investment risk fluctuations over the 
terms of GMP’s most recent alternative regulation plans.  We also value the transparency and 
simplicity of this approach.  However, we are open-minded about considering alternative 
formulas in the future.  We strongly encourage the Department and GMP to collaborate in 
advance of any future alternative regulation filings to evaluate potential alternatives to the 
current ROE formula.  The parties should consider whether there are alternative securities, such 
as a 30-year Treasury yield, or formulas that could be used to transparently adjust the ROE in a 
manner that reasonably reflects investor expectations. 
Debt Forecast Plan 
 
We also decline to authorize GMP’s proposed debt forecast process.  Section 108 
requires that: 
A domestic corporation subject to the jurisdiction of the Public Utility Commission 
shall not mortgage nor pledge any of its corporate property nor issue any stocks, 
bonds, notes, or other evidences of indebtedness without the consent of the Public 
Utility Commission given on petition and after opportunity for hearing of the 
corporation or its incorporators and a finding of the Commission that the proposed 
action will be consistent with the general good of the State. 
We requested that the parties provide legal briefing on whether GMP’s proposed debt forecast 
process is consistent with Section 108.  In response to this request, GMP asserts that its proposed 
approach “does not reduce Commission oversight of debt financing; rather, it shifts the review

and approval to the point where it is most meaningful—during comprehensive review of the 
FY27 rate case.”10  With respect to its legal argument, GMP points to Section 218d, which 
authorizes the Commission to approve alternative regulation plans that include “changes or 
additions to, waivers of, or alternatives to, traditional rate-making procedures, standards, and 
mechanisms.”  GMP also cites to prior Commission orders that establish precedent that Section 
108 does not “mandate a specific level of review of a financing petition” and that the 
Commission has previously authorized “blanket” financing approvals under Section 108.11 
 
We are not persuaded by GMP’s legal arguments.  A debt financing subject to Section 
108 involves a mortgage, pledged assets, or other “evidence of indebtedness.”  Although the 
issuance of debt ultimately affects GMP’s cost of service, Commission approval of a debt 
issuance is not a “traditional rate-making procedure[], standard[], and mechanism[].”  Instead, 
Section 108 approval constitutes a determination that the issuance of a financial instrument is 
consistent with the public good.  This is a different standard and different process than the 
traditional ratemaking requirements set out in 30 V.S.A. §§ 225-227 and our rate case 
precedents.  Accordingly, we decline to rely on Section 218d to authorize this request.   
 
To the extent that the Commission has authorized “blanket” Section 108 approval in the 
past, it has only done so in the context of authorizing de minimis regulation for hydroelectric 
merchant electric generators subject to federal regulation or competitive telecommunications 
providers.12  In these cases, the Commission stressed that de minimis Section 108 approval is 
justified where the following three factors are present: (1) there is a wholesale generator selling 
output into New England wholesale markets; (2) there is no Vermont-specific state interest to be 
protected by future financings; and (3) the case involves a competitive energy supplier that 
requires greater flexibility than a vertically integrated utility in responding to market conditions.  
None of these three factors is satisfied by GMP’s request.

Legal Standard 
 
The Commission has the responsibility under Vermont law to ensure that monopoly 
utility rates are “just and reasonable.”46  This standard reflects the principle that rates are not 
merely formulaic but instead are an estimate of the costs incurred by the utility to provide safe 
and reliable service while meeting all statutory requirements imposed on the utility.  Given the 
essential service they provide, electric utilities operate within a heavily regulated context, 
including regulatory expectations for safe and reliable electric service;47 federally regulated 
wholesale electricity markets and transmission reliability standards; and environmental policy 
requirements established in Vermont statute, such as the RES.48  
 
In evaluating a utility’s proposed rates, the Commission considers whether those rates 
provide the utility with a reasonable opportunity to recover its cost to serve customers.  In setting 
rates, the Commission’s role is not to manage the utility but instead to review the reasonableness 
of the utility’s decisions.49    
 
The Vermont Supreme Court explained the process for determining just and reasonable 
rates as follows: 
[T]he [Commission] determines the operating expenses and the “rate base”—the 
utility’s net plant investment—for the “test year,” usually the most recent full 
calendar year. . . .  The [Commission] then adjusts the rate base by modifying the 
test year rate base to reflect “known and measurable” changes in plant investment.

[Commission] is required to set rates that are just and reasonable.”).

electric service.

Discussion  
 
There are three essential steps in setting the weighted average cost of capital in a utility 
rate case.  First, we determine an appropriate capital structure.  Second, we determine the cost of 
each capital component.  Third, we determine the cost of each component according to its 
proportion of the total capital structure.  The sum of these weighted capital components is the 
weighted-average cost of capital.58

In this case, the parties have agreed that GMP’s cost of capital will be based on 50/50 
debt-to-equity ratio plus or minus 1%, which will be carried forward as part of the MYRP.  The 
parties have also agreed to the reasonableness of the debt included in GMP’s cost of service.  
Our resolution of the cost of capital issue, therefore, is based on resolving the parties’ dispute 
over the authorized ROE. 
For the authorized ROE component of a utility’s cost of service, our precedent is well 
settled that “[n]either the law nor regulatory precepts prescribe a specific methodology for 
setting the appropriate [ROE].”59   The Commission therefore has discretion in determining an 
appropriate rate level.60  The Commission has repeatedly emphasized that the critical element is 
the “reasonableness of the result” and not the methodology employed to reach it.61  The basic 
standard for an appropriate rate of ROE is as follows: 
A public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it to earn a return on the value 
of the property which it employs for the convenience of the public equal to that 
generally being made at the same time and in the same general part of the country 
on investments in other business undertakings which are attended by corresponding 
risks and uncertainties; but it has no constitutional right to profits such as are 
realized or anticipated in highly profitable enterprises or speculative ventures.  The 
return should be reasonably sufficient to assure confidence in the financial 
soundness of the utility and should be adequate, under efficient and economical 
management, to maintain and support its credit and enable it to raise the money 
necessary for the proper discharge of its public duties.62 
These principles have been incorporated into Vermont statute and have been endorsed 
repeatedly by the Vermont Supreme Court.63 
 
We begin our discussion on the authorized ROE issue by making clear that we are not 
wholly persuaded by either party’s evidence or arguments on the appropriate ROE.

GMP’s witness testified that a reasonable range for GMP’s ROE is approximately 9.91% to 
10.91%, with a weighted mean of approximately 10.41%.  Based on those analyses and GMP’s

Turning to GMP’s testimony, we find that GMP’s ROE-related evidence substantially 
understates the degree to which the MYRP shields GMP from downside financial risk.  We 
recognize that there are broader financial and macro-economic factors, including inflation and 
regulatory uncertainty at the federal level, that affect how investors perceive the relative risk of 
investing in regulated utilities.  We do not take issue with GMP’s testimony on these more 
fundamental macro-economic considerations, which by and large affect all utilities equally.   
 
GMP’s cost-of-capital witness, however, also placed a heavy emphasis on GMP’s own 
operational risks in determining an appropriate ROE for the company.  For example, the witness 
cited GMP’s construction-work-in-progress balance, unrecovered storm costs, regulatory lag, 
and other operational challenges as substantial financial risks for GMP even while it is operating 
under the MYRP.  We disagree with this aspect of GMP’s testimony.  Unless GMP is subjected 
to a statutory penalty or regulatory disallowance, the ESAM all but ensures that GMP’s actual 
ROE will remain within 100 basis points of its authorized ROE.  This structure offers strong 
protection for GMP’s downside risk.  The MYRP’s various other adjustors also largely ensure 
that GMP recovers—dollar-for-dollar—most of any unexpected costs or price volatility 
stemming from factors outside of GMP’s control, such as major storms or fluctuations in 
wholesale power and transmission costs.  Although these adjustors include various efficiency 
bands and deductibles, they are ultimately backstopped by the ESAM.  It is true that these 
components of the MYRP correspondingly limit GMP’s financial upside, but they offer a 
substantial degree of risk mitigation that is not present in traditional regulation in Vermont.  
From our perspective, GMP’s witness greatly overstated GMP’s business and operational risks 
while the MYRP is in place. 
 
GMP also criticizes the Department’s recommendation as being inconsistent with 
recently authorized ROEs for vertically integrated utilities in other jurisdictions.  Although we 
remain mindful of ROEs set by other jurisdictions, those determinations are not dispositive to 
our analysis.  Instead, our final determination on GMP’s ROE must be grounded in our own 
independent assessment of GMP’s relative risk and investor expectations.
